Human Faces Within Stone: My Life by Sergei Konenkov

Mostafa Auvi (মোস্তফা অভি) · 2026-11-01

Do we see only with our eyes, or do we also see with our minds? Eyes present the scene before us, but to feel the human sorrow, the wounds of time, and the long sighs of history hidden behind that scene, we need the mind as well. Where an ordinary person sees a block of stone, a sculptor sees a figure. His task is to free that figure from the stone. I kept returning to this thought while reading about the life and work of Sergei Timofeyevich Konenkov, the Russian sculptor.

Reading his autobiographical memoir My Life left me with a somewhat different experience. I felt closer to him than any formal biography of a famous artist would have brought me. A long-lived man is revisiting the turns of his life: first his childhood village, then the gatherings of artists in Moscow, then the turbulent days of revolution, and finally a workshop in distant America. As his memory moves, the landscape of his time changes with it. Within a single life, several Russias appear: the Russia of the tsars, the Russia of revolution, and the Soviet Union.

The most striking feature of Konenkov’s memoir is that he sees his own life as part of a larger history. His growing up, his development as an artist, his relationships with people, the political upheavals, and his long stay abroad all become part of his search for his own time. The book is therefore the autobiography of a sculptor, but it also becomes a record of one country’s social and cultural transformation.

Sergei Konenkov was born on 10 July 1874 in Karakovichi, a village in the Smolensk region. He came from a peasant family, though their circumstances were somewhat better than those of many destitute peasants. This distinction matters. His rural childhood, folk beliefs, woodwork, nature, and the lives of ordinary people all deeply shaped his artistic outlook later on.

To understand late nineteenth-century Russia, one must look at its villages. Although serfdom was abolished in 1861 under Tsar Alexander II, the peasants’ freedom remained incomplete. Land, debt, rent, and social inequality weighed heavily on their lives. Meanwhile, industry was expanding in the cities and a working class was emerging, yet the old land system and its many contradictions persisted in the countryside.

Konenkov, a child of this society, grew up very close to human labour, to nature, and to rural life. The peasant figures, the characters of Russian folk tales, and the natural strength of the human body that recur throughout his later work owe something to this early experience.

His path to becoming an artist was not a simple one. He first studied, then trained at the Moscow School of Painting, Sculpture, and Architecture, where he worked from 1892 to 1896. He later gained access to advanced art education in Saint Petersburg. His travels in Europe further broadened his artistic sensibility.

Reading about this education makes one thing very clear: an artist is formed through a combination of talent and practice, schooling, observation, and the ability to see the world anew. In Konenkov’s case, the folk experience of the village and formal academic training worked side by side. His roots lay in the soil of the Russian countryside, and his eyes were opened to the many currents of European art.

Among Konenkov’s early major works is Kamenevshchik, or The Stonebreaker, made in 1898. This sculpture brought him recognition in the art world, and for it he received the large silver medal of the Moscow school.

The title itself seems to contain a key to his artistic thinking. A worker is breaking stone. The posture of his body, the tension of his muscles, and the weight of his labour together make physical toil the subject of art. The worker appears as a person whose body holds strength, endurance, and the dignity of work.

Working people had been depicted in art before. What is significant in Konenkov’s work is that he found sculptural beauty in the everyday labour of ordinary people. To him, the human body was a marvellous construction of nature itself.

At this point the book raises an important question for the reader: does beauty exist only in the ornaments of aristocratic life? Can the body of a person exhausted by labour also be beautiful? When an artist shapes the figure of a worker with a hammer in hand, he is also redefining the conventional sense of beauty in society.

Konenkov’s work also clearly reflects Russian folk traditions. Wooden sculptures, characters from folk tales, mythological figures, and the relationship between humans and nature all hold an important place in his art. The folk imagination visible in works such as Firebird or Winged differs entirely from the imitation of Western academic sculpture. Here the imaginative power of Russian folk art is at work.

This reveals a distinctive quality in Konenkov as an artist. He received a modern art education, yet he kept hold of his cultural roots. This union of the two is what sets his art apart.

The Revolution of 1905 was an important moment in Konenkov’s life. Across Russia’s cities, workers, peasants, and ordinary people were rising against tsarist autocracy. Clashes, strikes, and political tension spread through Moscow as well. Konenkov was connected to the events of the time, and revolutionary sentiment left its mark on his art.

Yet to view his life merely as the career of a political propagandist would be an incomplete picture. His artistic life also made room for symbols, mythological imagination, folk heritage, the human body, and personal portraiture. Understanding the range of his art requires looking at all these dimensions together.

The Revolution of 1917 transformed Russia’s political and cultural life from the ground up. After the fall of the old order, the new state sought to connect art with public life. Under Lenin’s plan for monumental propaganda, efforts began to bring art into public spaces. Konenkov took part in the artistic work of this period.

On 1 May 1919, his monument to Stepan Razin was unveiled in Red Square in Moscow. Lenin delivered a speech at the opening ceremony. This event stands as a significant chapter in Konenkov’s artistic career.

Stepan Razin was a rebellious figure in Russian history. In the seventeenth century, he led peasant and Cossack uprisings against the ruling elite. His rebellion occupies a special place in Russian popular memory and historical imagination. When Konenkov gave this figure sculptural form, he was not merely reconstructing a historical individual. He was also creating a symbol of revolt, the longing for freedom, and the human protest against power.

Here the relationship between art and politics becomes important. During the revolution, the artist’s work became connected to the ideals of the state. But the meaning of a work of art extends beyond the intentions of its maker or the official interpretation of it. The historical memory of rebellion embodied in a figure like Razin can return with new meanings at different times.

Reading Konenkov’s life also brings the question of artistic freedom and political use to the surface. Art can speak on behalf of people, and the state can use art as a vehicle for its own message. Between these two lies the question of where the artist’s personal conscience and aesthetic sensibility stand. The book prompts this question as the reader moves through it.

Another compelling aspect of Konenkov’s memoir is his relationship with contemporary writers and artists. His workshop was visited by writers, poets, musicians, and people from the world of theatre. To understand the Moscow artistic life of that period, these relationships are particularly important.

His acquaintance and friendship with Maxim Gorky also appear in the memoir. Gorky was a major Russian writer who addressed working people, social inequality, and revolutionary consciousness. Konenkov’s art, too, featured the presence of ordinary people and their labour. Although their media differed, human life stood at the centre of both their creations.

Still, it would be wrong to equate the purposes of a writer and a sculptor. Gorky built human lives with words. Konenkov expressed human bodies and emotions through stone, wood, and other materials. Their creative languages were different, yet their interest in human beings brought them close.

Konenkov also had a relationship with the poet Sergei Yesenin. Yesenin’s poetry returns repeatedly to the Russian village, nature, love, separation, and a consciousness of mortality. The references to Yesenin in the memoir take the reader back into the literary atmosphere of that time.

The value of these sections lies in far more than their recounting of famous acquaintances. What matters most is how an artist saw other artists, how he exchanged ideas with them, and how he held their lives and work in his memory.

It is also important to keep in mind a natural limitation of autobiography. Memory is far more complex than a camera. It is coloured by a person’s own point of view. When recalling events from many years earlier, people often rearrange them in light of their later feelings, subsequent experiences, and the political climate of the time. For this reason, it is best to check the dialogues and judgments in any memoir against other sources. This caution makes the reader more aware and adds to the value of the book.

One of the most remarkable chapters of Konenkov’s life is his period in America. In late 1923, at the initiative of Anatoly Lunacharsky, the Soviet official responsible for education and culture, he travelled to the United States to take part in Russian and Soviet art exhibitions. The trip was meant to last a few months, but it stretched on for much longer. From 1924 to 1945 he lived and worked in New York.

If this long period is seen merely as a story of living abroad, its full significance is lost. A Russian sculptor was establishing his place in the artistic and intellectual life of America. There he was building a new audience for his work. He created portraits of various individuals, took part in exhibitions, and expanded his reputation as an artist.

Among the portraits he made during this time, the bust of Albert Einstein is particularly notable. In it one can see an attempt to capture the scientist’s facial structure, pensive expression, and personality. For a sculptor, portraiture is far more than outward likeness. The difficult task is to suggest a person’s inner nature through the lines of the face, the gaze of the eyes, the angle of the head, and the slight curve of the body.

Konenkov’s meeting with Einstein and the making of the portrait are an engaging part of his memoir. However, there is no reliable primary evidence for some of the admiring remarks that have been attributed to Einstein in connection with this portrait. Those statements therefore cannot be accepted as confirmed historical quotations.

During his years in America he was joined by his wife, Margarita Ivanovna Vorontsova. The two married in 1922. Margarita was an important companion throughout his life. The history of their relationship is also quite complex. Margarita later came into historical discussion through her association with Albert Einstein, and her political and intelligence-related role has been the subject of research.

This thread makes Konenkov’s personal life more complicated. An artist’s life is often more intricate and tangled than his artwork. Love, relationships, political connections, personal decisions, and the hidden currents of history all operate together there.

In 1945 Konenkov returned to the Soviet Union. He had spent roughly twenty-two years in America. Biographical accounts note that a special ship was arranged for his return. He brought with him the artworks and experiences of his long American years.

If this homecoming is explained only in terms of an emotional attachment to his homeland, the picture remains incomplete. State initiatives, political connections, and personal decisions all played a part in his return. In his memoir the artist explains this chapter from his own perspective. The reader’s task is to hold that account alongside the historical context.

Among Konenkov’s works, the 1923 sculpture Textile Worker is especially important for understanding his artistic vision. For the All-Russian Agricultural and Handicraft Exhibition in Moscow, he made several wooden sculptures, including Worker, Peasant Woman, and Textile Worker. The Textile Worker was made for the textile pavilion of that exhibition. The work is now preserved in the Tretyakov Gallery in Moscow.

The sculpture depicts a woman. In the body’s structure, the folds of the fabric, and the position of the hands, there is a certain rhythm. It presents a working woman and also reveals the sculptor’s own artistic inquiry. Using a material such as wood, he gave a complete form to the relationship between the body and the cloth.

What distinguishes this work is that the artist did not portray the working woman merely as a political symbol. Through her body’s structure, posture, and dress, he created a distinct language of beauty. If the work is viewed only as a celebration of labour, its sculptural qualities fade from view. If it is viewed only as physical beauty, its historical and social context disappears.

It has not been firmly established that Margarita was the model for this sculpture, so it is wise to be cautious about that claim. However, during the American period Konenkov is known to have created several female figures based on Margarita as a model.

This distinction matters when discussing the female body in Konenkov’s art. In his female sculptures one finds, on the one hand, a search for physical beauty and, on the other, traces of nature, mythological imagination, and personal relationships.

While reading My Life, one point stood out to me in particular. Konenkov recalls his life at a time when the Soviet state was interpreting its own history through a fixed ideological language. As a result, the personal memories in his autobiography sometimes blend with the vocabulary of state history.

Here the reader must pause and reflect. When an artist speaks of the revolution, is he simply describing what he saw, or does his later political experience shape that memory as well? When he speaks of Soviet society’s achievements, should the limitations and contradictions of that society also be kept in view alongside his assessment? These questions help us read the autobiography more deeply.

Konenkov’s life encompassed the fall of tsarism, the revolution, post-civil-war society, the new state’s cultural policies, and the experience of the Second World War. How an artist continued his work amid such vast change is itself a question worth considering.

The lasting value of his memoir lies in the fact that he was a direct participant in his own era. Yet even an eyewitness brings his own perspective. His memory and his interpretations are both important, and they are best read alongside other historical records.

A major lesson from world literature and art criticism is that one can love a creator, appreciate his work, and still question his limitations. These three responses complement one another and can coexist.

Konenkov lived a long life. He was born in 1874 and died in Moscow on 9 October 1971. In the later part of his life he received official recognition in the Soviet art world. He became a member of the Soviet Academy of Arts in 1954, was awarded the Lenin Prize in 1957, and in 1958 was given the title People’s Artist of the USSR. In 1964 he was named Hero of Socialist Labour.

If we divide his long life into a few scenes, we see a village, an art school, a workshop, a revolutionary city, a studio in New York, and finally a sculptor’s home in Moscow once again. Between these scenes, times changed, states changed, and patronage of the arts changed. Yet his exploration of the human form continued without interruption.

Throughout Konenkov’s memoir, the artist’s moral responsibility and his duty to humanity recur. This message connects with his artistic output. At different stages of his life he sculpted workers, peasants, historical figures, writers, scientists, and ordinary people. For him, the human being was a central subject of art.

But what does a duty to humanity mean? Should the artist speak on behalf of people, or should he present them in such a way that the viewer can see their lives anew? Konenkov’s work points clearly toward the second possibility. He shaped human bodies and faces so that each figure carries the individual alongside a sense of time.

Perhaps this is the artist’s greatest achievement. When a work moves beyond the boundaries of the individual and connects with the experience of others, it remains meaningful to new audiences.

Having finished My Life, I feel that the greatest resource in Konenkov’s life was his capacity to see time. He passed through a century in which people’s political identities, social positions, state structures, and the language of art changed again and again. He stood within that change. At times he became part of it, at times he witnessed it, and at times he interpreted it through his art.

His life suggests that an artist’s task is far more than making matter beautiful. His real work is to find within the visible world something that ordinary sight cannot easily perceive. In a worker’s body he sees the history of labour. In the figure of a rebel he sees the human longing for freedom. In a scientist’s face he finds depth of thought. In a woman’s body he sees nature, beauty, and the rhythm of life.

As I read, I also came to feel that the artist’s memory is itself a kind of sculpture. From the stone of time, he lifts some events into view while others remain hidden. He gives his lived life a particular shape. That shape contains his beliefs, his love, his resentments, his political position, and his personal limitations. To know the man, the reader must move through that act of construction.

This brings me back to the question with which I began: do we see only with our eyes, or with our minds as well? Looking at Konenkov’s life and art, it seems there is a long road between seeing with the eyes and understanding with the mind. That road is traveled through feeling, thought, experience, and questioning. His chisel cut the stone, but the human face he sought within that stone is the true signature of his art.

My Life is therefore far more than an account of a famous sculptor’s success to me. It has become a record of one person’s struggle with time, his construction of an artistic language, and his long effort to understand human life. After finishing the book, I was left with the sense that stone may wear away and the surface of a sculpture will bear the marks of time. Yet if an artist can truly see human life, then future generations who stand before his work will learn to recognise humanity anew.
